summary:
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a Union Territory of India and stands under India's national framework for transgender recognition and protection. No territory-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, so a visitor to the islands is assessed against the national position, which changed materially in March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. The bill amends the 2019 law and removes the self-identification route to legal recognition that had been affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014. Protests were held in Mumbai on the day of passage.

Recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, with recognition in practice narrowed to male and female categories plus those traditional identities. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme entirely. Critics warn that the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist.

Medical certification becomes a condition of identity recognition. Gender-affirming surgery requires certification by a medical board and a district authority. For a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification, this is a direct documents consequence: identity papers issued under the old route may not be reissued or amended on the same basis.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed and predates the amendment. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The territory was scored at the national position because the country dossier identified no deviation material enough to score separately, within a tolerance of ±0.02, and no division-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

The March 2026 bill was passed against a visible protest backdrop, with demonstrations reported in Mumbai, and its passage was still unresolved as to presidential assent when the sources were compiled. Contested framing surrounds it: the government casts the amendment as broadening welfare access and protection from trafficking, while the People's Union for Civil Liberties, rights campaigners and critics characterise it as a rollback that excludes most self-identifying trans and non-binary people.

The scale of the affected population is national rather than local: about two million transgender people live in India, so the narrowed recognition scheme bears on a very large community and on the identity documents a visitor may be asked to present.

Comparatively, the 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, a protection lost while the recognition scheme was also being narrowed. Independent country reporting runs partly contrary to activist accounts: the UK Home Office note of December 2025 describes police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, whereas documented checkpoint incidents in 2024 and 2026 show targeted handling of trans individuals by transport and aviation security.
localsOnly:
For residents of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, identity recognition runs through the national scheme as amended in March 2026: application is confined to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and to intersex people, and requires medical certification, with gender-affirming surgery conditional on medical-board and district-authority certification. Residents who self-identify as trans men, trans women, non-binary or gender-fluid outside those categories have no recognition route under the amended scheme.

Residents continue to access welfare schemes through the same national channels the government says the amendment widens, and residents retain standing to challenge the amendment or its implementing rules in court. The People's Union for Civil Liberties and other organisations have publicly opposed the bill, and litigation or advocacy by them is part of the resident-facing environment.

Residents are also covered by the protection machinery that exists independently of the amendment: the Madras High Court guidelines of 7 June 2021 on police sensitisation and the ban on conversion therapy, and the constitutional protections arising from the 2018 decriminalisation judgment and the non-discrimination grounds that include sex as interpreted to cover gender identity.

Resident-facing criminal protection is weaker than it was before 2024, since the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita dropped the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences. Communities report fear of more assaults under the new code, and there is no territory-specific enforcement record documenting how that plays out locally. The national population context, an estimated two million transgender people, frames the domestic scale of these rules.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill is unresolved in the sources: the bill was passed by both houses on 25 March 2026 and was awaiting assent, so the provisions described are not confirmed as in force.

No Andaman and Nicobar Islands-specific enforcement data, incident record, or administrative guidance on implementing the amended recognition rules is on file. Whether the territory's authorities apply the medical certification and district-authority procedures as described nationally is not sourced.

The status of identity documents already issued under the 2019 self-identification route is unresolved: the sources do not say whether existing certificates remain valid, are reissuable, or must be converted. The effect of the amendment on passport and airport procedures in this territory is likewise not sourced.

Local court jurisdiction, police conduct, and conversion-practice reports for the islands are not covered by the sources; the cited judicial guidance comes from the Madras and Allahabad High Courts and the Supreme Court, and the UK Home Office country note does not specify the islands separately.

The practical reach of the new coercion offences, including whether they have been used against trans people or their partners, is not documented in the available material.
